activities.caption: five cues that need no vanishing point
activities.name: perspCueMatch

config.prompt: Depth without geometry — match each cue to what it says:

pairs.right: an object cutting another off is in front — the strongest, earliest cue
of two similar objects, the larger reads nearer
higher on the surface reads farther — the Western ground-plane habit
surfaces get finer and denser with distance — pebbles shrink, grass compresses

config.why: Atmospheric perspective completes the set — air scatters blue light, so distance arrives lighter, bluer, less contrasted. Giotto's figures overlap and shade convincingly while their architecture refuses the window: the cues and the geometry are separable skills.

activities.caption: the mirror trick and its codification, in order
activities.name: perspDemoOrder

config.prompt: How the window arrived — assemble the sequence:
items: c. 1420s — Brunelleschi paints the Baptistry on a panel, drills a peephole at the vanishing point
The mirror: the painting reflected against the real building — viewers cannot tell them apart
c. 1427 — Masaccio's Trinity puts the new maths in a church
1435 — Alberti's De pictura codifies the picture as a window: the costruzione legittima
config.why: A city of surveyors, cartographers and pricing merchants wanted the world calculable — and got a picture system to match; within decades every trained painter in Europe was converging lines.

activities.anchor: The whole apparatus rests on one fact
activities.caption: one-, two- or three-point? file the jobs
activities.name: perspSysSort

config.prompt: Choose the system by the subject's geometry — file each case:

items.label: the hallway or road — one face parallel to the picture plane
the classroom construction: front rectangle, mark the point, project the corners
the corner of a building — only the verticals stay parallel
place the near vertical edge, project to both points on the horizon
the worm's-eye and bird's-eye drama of film posters — best rationed

config.why: The horizon line is always the viewer's eye level — the projection of infinitely distant sight-lines: we look down on every surface below it and up at everything above it.

activities.anchor: the first construction line is the same
activities.caption: one belief in this horizon briefing is wrong
activities.name: perspHorSpot

config.prompt: One belief in this horizon briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Draw the horizon line at the height of your eyes, wherever you are.
Every tabletop below it recedes upward toward the horizon.
Every ceiling edge above it recedes downward toward the horizon.
A windowless interior at midnight has no horizon, so skip the construction.
Landscape or hallway, the first construction line is the same.
config.correction: The horizon of a drawing is the viewer's eye level, projected through the scene — it exists indoors, windowless, at midnight; the Earth's edge has nothing to do with it.
config.why: Set the horizon first and everything follows mechanically — tops below it slope up toward it, undersides above it slope down toward it.

config.prompt: Two calibration tools — drag the divider:

before.label: pencil-and-thumb
before.text: arm locked, compare any width against any height — comparative, never absolute; arm length varies, ratios transfer

after.label: sight-size
after.text: subject and paper appear the same size from one fixed spot; step back repeatedly to compare — the rigidity is the feature, and a fixed viewpoint makes perspective automatic

config.why: The unifying habit is the fixed viewpoint: almost every perspective error in observational drawing is really a viewpoint error — the head drifted, and the window quietly changed.

activities.anchor: zooming is not the same as walking
activities.caption: three jobs, three projection systems
activities.name: perspProjBranch

config.root: A workshop needs a drawing of a new machine part that they can measure from. Which projection do you reach for?

choices.label: Linear perspective — the window
choices.feedback: Convincing, but converging edges destroy comparability — measurements do not transfer off the page.

choices.label: Isometric or axonometric — keep all parallels parallel
choices.feedback: No convergence, no size falloff — depth legible and distances measurable, which is exactly why engineers declined the window.

choices.label: A handscroll convention — the moving viewpoint
choices.feedback: A cinematic, time-travelling choice — made for journeys, useless for a workshop measurement.

window.text: The Renaissance agreement: one viewer, one eye, one moment — persuasive, and built for pictures, not parts.

iso.text: The architect's and game-designer's drawing — measurable truth traded against depth drama.

scroll.text: Song-dynasty logic: the scroll unrolls through time and the eye travels the journey — no single vanishing point exists.

config.why: Panofsky's formulation is the adult position: perspective is a symbolic form — a historically specific decision, a remarkably persuasive agreement rather than truth. And the lens lesson holds: viewpoint, not focal length, determines the look.

activities.caption: true or false — shadows and the anamorphic trick
activities.name: perspShadowJudge

statements.s: A figure without a contact shadow floats like a sticker.
statements.why: A shadow anchors the object to its surface and encodes the light's direction — depth information twice over.

statements.s: Shadows read most truthful when drawn darker than instinct suggests.
statements.why: The opposite: beginners almost always over-darken them — draw them lighter than instinct suggests.

statements.s: A shadow across a step bends with the step.
statements.why: Shadows fall on the surface and obey that surface's geometry — darkest at contact, softest at distance.

statements.s: Holbein's skull in The Ambassadors is a casual distortion.
statements.why: Anamorphosis is perspective run deliberately wrong — computed, not casual, snapping into legibility only from one glancing viewpoint.

config.text: The eye only resolves sharply at the centre of gaze; cameras imitate this with %%0%%. Painters knew the effect centuries earlier — Leonardo's %%1%% softens distant mountains into air, and the tilt-shift effect inverts it: blur a real landscape's top and bottom and the brain reads a %%2%%.
config.hint: One is the camera's word, one Leonardo's, one what the trick makes you see.
